en: To come before in time; to precede
hook: ANTE = before. Dated BEFORE.
story: The ruins of Mahasthangarh antedate the Mughal empire by more than a thousand years. The city existed long before most famous kingdoms of the region. To antedate is to come earlier in time. Synonyms: predate, precede. Ante means before, as in antecedent.

en: To send someone away officially as punishment; to get rid of
hook: BANISH: make them VANISH.
story: In the old story, the king banished his own son to the forest for fourteen years. Today, Mitu banished her phone from the bedroom to sleep better. To banish is to expel or send away. You can banish fears, doubts, and distractions too.

en: To restrain or control; also, to show resentment or anger
bn: সংযত করা; লাগাম টানা, ক্ষোভ প্রকাশ করা
hook: BRIDLE: the straps on a horse's head that hold it back.
story: Arif had to bridle his anger when the shopkeeper insulted him; he took a deep breath and walked away. A bridle is the harness that controls a horse. To bridle is to restrain. Tricky: it can also mean to bristle with anger, as in 'she bridled at the insult.'

en: To act according to a rule, request, or command
hook: COMPLY: COMPLETE what's asked.
story: The new law required all buses to have speed limiters. Most companies complied within a month; those that didn't were fined. To comply is to obey or conform. Compliance with rules keeps everyone safe.

en: Sad and disappointed
hook: CREST-FALLEN: a rooster whose proud crest has drooped.
story: Tanvir had prepared for months. When the results showed he had missed the scholarship by just two points, he walked out crestfallen, head down, shoulders slumped. Crestfallen means deeply disappointed, like a proud rooster whose crest has fallen. It's the opposite of elated.

en: To reduce or cut short
hook: CUR-TAIL: cut the TAIL short.
story: When the cyclone warning came, the school curtailed its sports day, ending it after just two events. The government also curtailed spending to save money. To curtail is to cut short or reduce. Curfews curtail freedom of movement.

en: To make clear; to explain
hook: E-LUCID-ATE: make it LUCID (clear).
story: The students were confused about photosynthesis, so the teacher elucidated it with a simple diagram: sunlight in, sugar and oxygen out. Suddenly, everyone understood. To elucidate is to explain and make clear. It's a favorite GRE verb for what good writers do.

en: To escape or avoid, especially by cleverness or trickery
hook: EVADE: like an EVASIVE dodge.
story: The businessman evaded taxes for years by hiding money in foreign accounts. When reporters asked him about it, he evaded the question by talking about charity. To evade is to escape or avoid cleverly. Tax evasion is illegal; tax avoidance can be legal.

en: Lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible and ineffective
hook: FECK-LESS: 'feck' is old Scottish for effect. No effect at all.
story: The feckless manager never made decisions, blamed others for every failure, and disappeared whenever problems arose. The team eventually stopped asking him anything. Feckless means irresponsible and incompetent. A feckless government fails to act in a crisis.

en: To become worse, especially through neglect; to rot
hook: FESTER: like an untreated wound that grows worse.
story: Rafi ignored a small cut on his foot until it festered, swollen and infected. His anger toward his brother festered the same way, silently growing worse for years. To fester is to worsen through neglect. Unresolved problems fester.

en: Attacking cherished beliefs or established traditions
hook: ICON-O-CLAST: one who smashes ICONS.
story: The iconoclastic young director made a film questioning everything society held sacred: marriage customs, exam culture, and hero worship. Critics either loved or hated it. Iconoclastic means challenging cherished beliefs. Originally, iconoclasts literally smashed religious images.

en: To confine or imprison within walls
hook: IM-MURE: 'mur' is wall (mural). Walled in.
story: In legends, the cruel king immured his enemies inside palace walls, sealing them alive. In modern terms, Nadia immured herself in her room for exam month, coming out only for meals. To immure is to shut someone in, as if behind walls.

en: To create or perform without preparation
hook: IMPROVISE: IM-PRO-VISE, not foreseen (pro-vise), done on the spot.
story: When the projector broke during her presentation, Sara improvised: she drew her charts on the whiteboard and told the story from memory. The audience loved it even more. To improvise is to make something up on the spot. Jazz musicians improvise their solos.

en: To restrain, hinder, or prevent
hook: INHIBIT: keeps you IN, holding you back.
story: Fear of making mistakes inhibited Tanvir from speaking English in class, even though he knew the answers. Certain medicines inhibit the growth of bacteria. To inhibit is to restrain or block. Inhibitions are feelings that hold you back socially.

en: Impossible to understand or interpret
hook: IN-SCRUTABLE: can't be SCRUTINIZED.
story: The poker player's face was inscrutable: no smile, no frown, no clue whether he held a great hand or nothing. Nobody could read him. Inscrutable means impossible to understand. It's a synonym of enigmatic.

en: To treat someone as a celebrity
bn: বীরের মতো সম্মান করা; তারকা বানিয়ে দেওয়া
hook: LIONIZE: treated like the LION, king of the jungle.
story: After winning the international math olympiad, the shy village girl was lionized: TV interviews, reception ceremonies, and her face on every newspaper. To lionize is to treat as a celebrity or hero. Society often lionizes the wrong people, though.

en: Dull and tedious because of lack of variety
hook: MONO-TONE: one tone, over and over.
story: The factory job was monotonous: putting the same bolt into the same hole, eight thousand times a day. Arif felt his brain switching off. Monotonous means dull and repetitive. A monotonous voice speaks in one unchanging tone. Synonyms: humdrum, tedious.

en: Strange or unusual; belonging exclusively to one person or place
hook: PECULIAR: PECULIAR things are PECULIARLY yours.
story: There was a peculiar smell in the kitchen: burnt sugar mixed with old socks. Mitu's family also has a peculiar habit, saying 'Bismillah' before turning on the generator. Peculiar means strange, or distinctive to a particular person or place.

en: To plan something, often a crime, in advance
hook: PRE-MEDITATE: MEDITATE on it BEFORE doing it.
story: The police discovered that the robbery was premeditated: the thieves had studied the guard's schedule for weeks and bought tools in advance. To premeditate is to plan beforehand. Premeditated murder is punished more severely than a crime of passion.

en: Recklessly extravagant or wasteful; shamelessly immoral
hook: PROFLIGATE: PRO at wasting.
story: The profligate heir spent his father's fortune in three years: luxury cars, endless parties, and gambling in Singapore. When the money ran out, so did his friends. Profligate means recklessly wasteful, a synonym of prodigal and spendthrift.

en: To restore friendly relations; to make two things consistent
hook: RE-CONCILE: bring back to COUNCIL, back together.
story: After ten years of silence, the two brothers reconciled at their mother's sickbed, hugging and crying. Later, an accountant reconciled the bank statements, making the numbers match. To reconcile is to restore harmony or to make things consistent.

en: To improve by making small changes; to remove impurities
hook: RE-FINE: make it FINE again and again.
story: Rafi refined his statement of purpose over twelve drafts, cutting weak sentences and sharpening every line. Factories refine sugar the same way, removing impurities until it's pure white. To refine is to improve or purify through small changes.

en: To voluntarily give up or let go
hook: RELINQUISH: RELease and finISH.
story: At seventy, the founder finally relinquished control of the company to his daughter. It was hard to let go after fifty years. To relinquish is to give up willingly. You can relinquish power, a claim, or your grip on a rope.

en: To think deeply about something
hook: RUMINATE: like a cow chewing cud, chewing a thought over and over.
story: Sitting by the river, Tanvir ruminated on his future: stay in Bangladesh, or go abroad? He turned the question over and over for hours. To ruminate is to think deeply, like a cow chewing its cud. Too much rumination on mistakes causes anxiety.

en: Nervous and easily frightened; unpredictable
hook: SKITTISH: like a SKITTERING kitten, jumps at every sound.
story: The stray cat was skittish; it ran away every time someone moved, even when Nadia held out food. Investors were skittish too, selling shares at the slightest bad news. Skittish means nervous and easily scared.

en: More than needed; unnecessary
hook: SUPER-FLUOUS: flows (flu) OVER (super) the top.
story: The editor deleted half of Arif's adjectives: 'very extremely big huge' became 'huge.' The rest were superfluous. Superfluous means unnecessary, more than needed. A superfluous remark adds nothing to the conversation.

en: Giving a brief general summary or overview
hook: SYN-OPTIC: seeing (optic) everything together (syn). A SYNOPSIS.
story: Before diving into details, the professor gave a synoptic view of the semester: five main topics, one diagram, and ten minutes. Students finally saw the big picture. Synoptic means providing a general summary. A synopsis is a brief outline of a story.

en: Complete with regard to every detail
hook: THOROUGH: goes THROUGH everything.
story: Before submitting her application, Mitu did a thorough check: every document, every date, every spelling. She found two mistakes that could have cost her admission. Thorough means complete and careful in every detail. Its opposite is cursory.

en: Thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
hook: VISIONARY: has a VISION of the future.
story: Fifty years ago, a visionary teacher dreamed of a university in his poor district. People laughed. Today, that university has ten thousand students. A visionary thinks boldly about the future. Visionary can also mean idealistic but impractical, depending on context.

en: Expressing opinions loudly and forcefully
hook: VOCI-FEROUS: a VOICE that's FEROCIOUS.
story: The cricket fans were vociferous in their criticism of the selectors, shouting outside the board office and flooding social media. Vociferous means loudly and forcefully expressing opinions. A vociferous critic makes sure everyone hears.
